newsitem.title: USA: Thailand can still issue debt with ease-US experts.
newsitem.headline: Thailand can still issue debt with ease-US experts.

text.p: Thailand's financial woes are not likely to deprive the country of funding access to the international capital markets, U.S. experts said.
International banks -- especially Japanese banks -- with long-term commitments in Thailand would keep credit lines open and bond investors regard Thailand as a low risk, they said.
Thailand plans to raise $10 billion through bank borrowing and bond issuance to replenish its reserves, which were severely depleted during its defense against speculative attacks on its currency.
The baht was allowed to float last week on July 2, resulting in a 15-percent devaluation.

"Thailand is a large country with high potential (for growth)," said Gregory Fager, director of the Asia division at the Institute of International Finance. "You have creditors who are committed to do business there."

A case in point is the Japanese banks, which, despite their own bad loan problems, have not flinched from lending to the Thai market, Fager said. It is estimated that half of Thailand's foreign debt is held by Japanese creditors.
A core group of two dozen international banks would keep the credit line open, which would provide stability for Thailand to pursue the structural adjustment, Fager said.

Ismail Dalla, president of Washington Asset Management, agreed that the risk of a Thai default was remote because Thailand has some $30 billion in reserves, enough to cover six months of imports. The devaluation would shrink the current account deficit as the imports drop and export rise, he added.
At this juncture, the International Monetary Fund could lubricate the credit mechanism of private lenders by conferring its seal of approval of reforms, he said.

After Thailand abandoned the foreign exchange regime that fixed the baht's value on a basket of major currencies, the government has asked the IMF for technical assistance on how to manage the floating exchange rate and on the consolidation of the financial sector.
"IMF gives credibility to the sequencing of the reforms," he said, adding that the IMF could help set the policy agenda to expedite the reforms through the Thai political process.
Market sources in New York said the sentiment of bond investors toward Thailand was cautiously optimistic.
A friendly U.S. interest rate environment and euphoria over surging Thai equities after the devaluation gave a warm glow to the battered Thai Yankee bond.
"If Thailand were to issue bonds now, they would sell well," said a syndicate manager.
But investors would ask for a higher risk premium now than three months ago when the Kingdom of Thailand sold $600 million in 10-year Yankee debt on April 10.
Priced at 90 basis points (bps) over U.S. Treasuries, the spread was currently bid at 95 bps. It traded as wide as 106/107 bps prior to the devaluation.

A Thai government official said a total of $10.0 billion in new debt would be raised: $5.0 billion from bank loans, and $5.0 billion from bond issuance in two tranches. He did not indicate when the funds would be raised.
While Thai sovereign debt was considered solid, corporate bonds have fallen out of favor among U.S. investors. Of the $85 billion foreign debt of Thailand, $66 billion is owned by the private sector.
Hart Woodson, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, said the devaluation would highlight the credit problems as the the burden of servicing foreign debt increases.
He expected the selling pressure to step up before July 23, the deadline for financial institutions to disclose their bad loans.
